chunks.text:
Hi Jesse,
Another year of dental school. Another year of you doing the thing: the grind, the exams, the clinics, the everything. You already know. But I’m going to say it anyway.
Last year I wrote about our late-night conversations, the endless riffing on what it means to be a man in this particular moment of history. We quoted Marcus Aurelius at each other like a secret handshake. This year, those conversations deepened. We talked about relationships in the specific way people talk when they’re actually in it, when the stakes are real and the questions don’t have clean answers. The Hinge stream, and the late talks.
Accept the things to which fate binds you, and love the people with whom fate brings you together, but do so with all your heart.Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.39 (popular rendering)
That line hits differently when you’re actually trying to do it.1 Loving with all your heart sounds simple until you realize it requires choosing, and the daily discipline of attention and repair.

Alain de Botton argues for a philosophy of pessimism about love.2 The romantic myth tells us we have to find the right person, and everything will work out. Compatibility is something you discover. Botton says that’s backwards: “Compatibility is an achievement of love; it must not be its precondition.” You make yourselves compatible through the slow, unglamorous work of understanding each other and repairing ruptures. The work never ends.
In The Course of Love he writes: “pronouncing a lover ‘perfect’ can only be a sign that we have failed to understand them.” Real love begins after the illusion breaks, after you see the person clearly and choose them anyway, because you’ve decided that this is the imperfection you’re willing to work with.
Rilke puts it differently, but he’s circling the same thing:
Love consists in this, that two solitudes protect and touch and greet each other.Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, letter 7 (1904)
Two solitudes. The romantic myth says you’re incomplete until someone completes you. Rilke is more/less emphasizing that you have to be whole first. You have to be a solitude worth protecting. And then love becomes two complete people meeting, each standing guard over the other’s separateness.

I think about our conversations on what it means to be a man, and I realize we were really talking about this. The stoics were against being captured by emotion, letting circumstance dictate your inner state. Marcus Aurelius wrote lovingly about his wife. Seneca’s letters are full of tenderness. The point was to make love something you do.
bell hooks says it bluntly: thinking of love “as an action rather than a feeling” is how anyone using the word “automatically assumes accountability and responsibility.”3 That’s the stoic insight translated into relationship terms. It’s the same discipline you bring to dental school: showing up when you don’t feel like it, doing the reps.
For one human being to love another human being: that is perhaps the most difficult task that has been entrusted to us, the ultimate task, the final test and proof.Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, letter 7 (Stephen Mitchell translation)

I’m proud of who you’re becoming. The dental school grind is shaping you, yes, but so are the relationship convos where we try to figure out what it means to love well. You’re doing the reps. That’s all any of us can do.
I’m here whenever you need me. In the real way: if something breaks, if you’re exhausted, if you need to talk through a relationship problem at 2am. You don’t need an occasion to reach out. I don’t need one to pick up.
You know where to find me.

remarque


the line circulates in this wording online. george long’s translation of 6.39 reads: “adapt thyself to the things with which thy lot has been cast: and the men among whom thou hast received thy portion, love them, but do it truly, sincerely.” ↩


alain de botton, the course of love (2016). the compatibility line and the “philosophy of pessimism” are from his NYT piece “why you will marry the wrong person” (28 may 2016), the most-read article in the times that year. the core insight: romantic love has been a disaster because it taught us to expect perfection instead of preparing us for the work. ↩
